segments.title: Naval procurement as economic stimulus
segments.body: Interwar navies without treaty limits would receive more investment, though the extra spending would not prevent the Great Depression. Warships offered governments a familiar way to support industry while publicly avoiding direct economic management. A major ship distributed orders among yards, machinery firms, fittings suppliers, furniture makers, and local employers. Naval procurement could therefore move public money through a wide supply chain with relatively few additional uniformed personnel.

evidence.note: A no-treaty scenario would increase naval investment without stopping the Great Depression.
Navies required relatively few service personnel while distributing orders for ship systems and fittings across the country.
Tillman's interest in Charleston employment illustrates the local political incentives behind naval procurement.

segments.summary: Naval building could spread industrial work during economic downturns without curing the Great Depression.

segments.title: Senator Tillman and Charleston Navy Yard patronage
segments.body: Senator Tillman understood naval procurement as local political economy. Employment at Charleston Navy Yard supported workers and the surrounding community. It also protected Tillman's electoral position, making the yard a direct example of military spending used as political patronage. Shipbuilding decisions could serve national industrial policy and a politician's local interests at the same time.

evidence.note: Charleston Navy Yard employment supported Tillman's local political position.

segments.summary: Charleston Navy Yard shows how naval employment could support a local economy while reinforcing a senator's political position.

segments.title: Why Anglo-American war plans did not make war likely
segments.body: Britain and the United States studied one another because each was the only plausible peer for testing a worst-case naval plan. Their exercises nevertheless concentrated on Japan, while the Anglo-American plans remained staff work rather than evidence of an approaching conflict. Dense diplomatic, financial, family, and imperial ties gave both governments strong reasons to negotiate. Either side would lose infrastructure and global standing even if it technically won a war.

evidence.note: Anglo-American plans remained theoretical, while exercises focused on the more likely Japanese opponent.
Either side would lose infrastructure and global standing even if it technically won a war.

segments.summary: Anglo-American war plans show worst-case staff work without the diplomatic conditions needed to cause a war.

segments.title: How staff papers gave the Army influence over policy
segments.body: Neglect of staff work left the prewar Admiralty poorly placed to explain its strategic priorities to politicians and civil servants. The Army circulated reports, scenarios, and operational papers that made its assumptions familiar to those audiences. A senior naval officer's personal advocacy could not match the reach of sustained written work by a large staff. By the interwar period, the Admiralty had a functioning staff producing contingency plans.

evidence.note: Admiralty neglect of staff work contrasted with Army circulation of planning papers and the later interwar naval staff.

segments.summary: Written staff work helped the Army establish its strategic assumptions among policymakers while the prewar Admiralty struggled to present its own case.

segments.title: The Sable Island feint in Anglo-American war planning
segments.body: American war planning anticipated a fleet encounter near Sable Island off Canada. The British plans described here used that expectation to propose a feint toward Canada, drawing the shorter-ranged American fleet north before approaching from another direction. American long-range maritime patrol makes the practical success of that maneuver uncertain. Both navies explored fighting each other in theoretical war games, while their fleet exercises concentrated on Japan.

evidence.note: Sable Island, a British feint toward Canada, uncertainty about American maritime patrol, and Japan as the fleet-exercise opponent.

segments.summary: The proposed British feint near Canada shows how a theoretical war plan could exploit an opponent's expectations without making that opponent the focus of fleet exercises.

segments.title: How shipbuilding could accelerate radar, welding, and gunnery
segments.body: Naval spending reaches into the research base behind a warship. Different steels and armor require metallurgical work and production development, while ships place technically skilled personnel beside machinery that can be modified in service. Continued long-range gunnery work might accelerate radar rangefinding, although earlier development cannot be established. Navies could justify investment in welding through possible savings in displacement and improvements in armor integrity, even when merchant operators found the unfamiliar technology too expensive. A qualitative race would also encourage work on loading systems, recoil effects, shells, and armor. The economic effect therefore reaches beyond jobs in the building yard.

evidence.note: Continuous naval work could support steel research and shipboard technical skills, while long-range gunnery might accelerate radar development.
Welding, armament mechanisms, recoil effects, armor, and shell development.

segments.summary: Continuous capital-ship work supports research in metallurgy, radar, welding, armament, armor, and machinery as well as employment.

segments.title: Shipboard workshops and the possibility of earlier radar
segments.body: Cruisers and larger warships carried machinists and workshop equipment, including lathes, to make components needed to keep the ship running. Skilled personnel working close to that machinery could also adapt equipment in service. This combination offered a practical setting for rapid technical development. Continued capital-ship construction might increase demand for accurate long-range gunnery measurements and encourage earlier radar rangefinding. Radar could supplement optical rangefinders and observation of shell splashes, but its earlier arrival remains a proposed consequence whose timing cannot be known.

evidence.note: Machinists, lathes, and repair workshops aboard cruisers and larger ships supported equipment modification.
Continued capital-ship building might encourage radar rangefinding, with the acceleration explicitly left uncertain.

segments.summary: Shipboard machinists could modify equipment at sea, while continued long-range gunnery development might create stronger demand for radar.

segments.title: Reducing gunfire shock so crews could keep working
segments.body: Gunfire transmitted shock through the ship and affected the people directing its weapons. One early application of shock-absorber research was reducing those effects on guns, structures, and crews. Reverberation could disorient personnel and interfere with their duties. Changes to seating were therefore considered as a way to help gun crews continue working effectively during firing.

evidence.note: Shock absorption and crew seating were considered to reduce gunfire-induced disorientation and preserve working effectiveness.

segments.summary: Gunfire shock could impair the crew's work, giving recoil and seating research an operational purpose.

segments.title: Washington Treaty shock to shipyards
segments.body: Large warships drew on engines, boilers, refrigeration, fittings, and the skilled people who designed and installed them. Steady orders kept yards able to bid for merchant construction and retain experienced staff during downturns. The Washington Naval Treaty removed current and future capital-ship work from that industrial system. Britain's County-class cruiser orders helped yards and replaced cruisers worn out during the war. A 10,000-ton cruiser, however, could not supply the work of a capital ship of 45,000 tons or more. Britain needed those cruisers anyway, so their construction left the loss of capital-ship orders largely unfilled.

evidence.note: Ship systems, machinery, and national labor effects behind warship construction.
Steady orders kept yards able to bid for merchant construction and retain experienced staff during downturns.
County-class cruisers were needed to replace worn-out ships, and their smaller scale could not replace the cancelled capital-ship work.

segments.summary: The Washington Naval Treaty abruptly cut capital-ship work, damaging yards and skilled labor pipelines.

segments.title: Why continuous warship orders preserve industrial skills
segments.body: Continuous procurement differs from a surge-and-cut industrial policy. Regular warship orders give major yards enough security to invest in technology and use that capacity when bidding for merchant construction. They also retain experienced designers, tradespeople, and production knowledge through downturns instead of dismissing them. Rebuilding that workforce for a later procurement surge would cost more and take longer. Industrial continuity is therefore an economic benefit apart from the headline number of ships built.

evidence.note: Secure warship work supports merchant bids, technology investment, and retention of experienced personnel during downturns.
Steady throughput avoids the long-term cost of repeatedly cutting and rebuilding procurement capacity.

segments.summary: Steady naval work helps shipyards retain skilled labor, adopt new technology, and compete for merchant contracts without expensive cycles of collapse and reconstruction.

segments.title: A qualitative Anglo-American race in capital ships
segments.body: British postwar gun development, American 16-inch construction, and Japanese industrial limits point to a qualitative race rather than a simple numerical arms race. Britain might emphasize speed and global range. The United States could emphasize gun power and coastal defense, allowing both navies to claim advantages in different categories. Japan could pursue its 8-8 plan only at the pace its yards and supporting industry permitted. The result resembles prestige competition and technical one-upmanship more than a direct march toward Anglo-American war.

evidence.note: A qualitative Anglo-American competition could center on British gun choices, American design disputes, and competing battlecruiser categories.
Japanese production limits differed from possible British and American building rhythms and design priorities.

segments.summary: Without treaty limits, Britain and the United States could compete over gun power, speed, and range without treating one another as likely wartime enemies.

segments.title: British gun experiments and the lessons drawn from German weapons
segments.body: British designers examined German guns after the war and combined those findings with their own construction methods. Lessons drawn too quickly from early tests led to mistakes in the combination of design approaches, including choices involving light shells. Further testing exposed problems after production was already well advanced. The resulting 16-inch weapons had shortcomings without being wholly ineffective. Earlier British work had pursued larger versions of Greenboy shells for 16.5-inch and potentially 18-inch guns, offering another possible direction for continued development.

evidence.note: Criticism of the fusion of British and German gun-design methods and light-shell decisions, with an explicit rejection of wholly ineffective 16-inch weapons.
Earlier British interest in 16.5-inch and potentially 18-inch versions of Greenboy shells.

segments.summary: Misread early tests could shape gun production before later trials exposed the weaknesses in the chosen approach.

segments.title: Iowa's gun-weight dispute and the battleship spectrum
segments.body: The Bureau of Ordnance expected to reuse an earlier gun for Iowa, while the Bureau of Ships wanted lighter guns and turrets to meet the ship's speed requirement. That dispute illustrates how armament weight affects the rest of a capital-ship design. The classification used here places fast battleships and battlecruisers along a spectrum of protection, speed, and mission. Iowa remains a fast battleship, while Hood's post-Jutland alterations leave it a battlecruiser because a further shift would require a complete redesign. G3 sits near the boundary between the categories. Lexington's emphasis on speed and its intended role place it closer to the cruiser end.

evidence.note: Conflicting American bureau expectations for Iowa's guns and turrets in a fast battleship design.
Hood, G3, and Lexington placed on a capital-ship spectrum according to mission, protection, and speed.

segments.summary: Gun and turret weight shaped Iowa's design, while Hood, G3, and Lexington illustrate different balances within the capital-ship spectrum.

segments.title: War debt, reparations, and the Depression
segments.body: Britain's financial exhaustion, in this interpretation, resulted from the cumulative effect of two world wars, the Great Depression, and the abrupt end of Lend-Lease. The no-treaty scenario still operates inside the financial aftermath of World War I. Germany borrowed American money to pay reparations to Britain, which used those receipts to repay its own American debts. When German reparations stopped, Britain also suspended its payments to the United States. This circular system helps explain why naval construction could soften an economic downturn without repairing the deeper international debt structure.

evidence.note: Cumulative pressures on Britain's finances and the circular system of American loans, German reparations, and British debt repayments.

segments.summary: The interwar loans and reparations cycle limits how much extra naval spending could change the wider economic crisis.

segments.title: Fleet choices without Washington limits
segments.body: Britain could return to a familiar rhythm of ordering capital ships and keeping roughly eight yards busy across rolling programs. The American case is less straightforward because Republican funding politics could threaten completion of ships already ordered as well as further construction after the South Dakotas and Lexingtons. Japan might finish more of the 8-8 fleet sequence before making carriers the priority. Older Royal Navy 15-inch ships could remain active while 13.5-inch ships moved into reserve. Some of the newer battlecruisers might pass to Dominion or imperial service as replacements entered the British fleet.

evidence.note: Britain returning to repeated capital-ship orders and keeping about eight yards busy.
American political support for naval spending was uncertain, including completion of existing orders and funding for later ships.
Japanese 8-8 fleet sequencing and possible Royal Navy redistribution of older capital ships.

segments.summary: A no-Washington scenario contrasts Britain's steady capital-ship rhythm with American politics and Japanese fleet-plan pressures.

segments.title: Carriers, cruisers, and postwar employment
segments.body: The no-treaty counterfactual changes more than battleship totals. France and Italy might keep some large ships in slow production for national pride, employment, and postwar social stability. Wages circulating through their communities could help families support wounded and traumatized returning servicemen, even when shipyards were unsuitable workplaces for those veterans. Without Lexington and Saratoga as treaty conversions, the United States may have to move from Langley toward a purpose-built carrier. The Royal Navy would still have strong incentives to seek a new station flagship type beyond its existing large light cruisers.

evidence.note: Low-rate French and Italian capital-ship production could provide local wages that helped families support disabled or traumatized veterans, despite the limitations of shipyard employment for those men.
Without Lexington and Saratoga as treaty conversions, the United States may have to move from Langley toward a purpose-built carrier.
Aging armored cruisers and expensive battlecruisers leave a station-flagship requirement that Hawkins-type large light cruisers cannot fill.

segments.summary: Without treaty conversions, carrier and cruiser development could follow different paths while yards supply postwar employment.

segments.title: Sloops and cutters after the destroyer-building surge
segments.body: Wartime shipbuilding would not continue at the same rate for every ship type after 1918. Destroyer production would slow after its enormous wartime surge, leaving governments to find other useful work for yards and smaller-warship supply chains. British sloops and United States Coast Guard cutters are plausible alternatives. Construction priorities would still differ by ship type in a world without naval treaties.

evidence.note: A postwar slowdown in destroyer building could leave more work for British sloops and American Coast Guard cutters.

segments.summary: A postwar pause in destroyer orders could redirect British and American construction toward sloops and Coast Guard cutters.

segments.title: Why distant stations could still require a new heavy cruiser
segments.body: Aging armored cruisers would eventually need replacement as station flagships. Battlecruisers were becoming too large and expensive for routine deployment to many distant stations. Hawkins-type large light cruisers were also judged unsuitable for that flagship role. This requirement could lead Britain to develop a new heavy cruiser even without treaty limits, with other navies responding to the British design.

evidence.note: Aging armored cruisers, increasingly expensive battlecruisers, and the limitations of Hawkins-type ships could prompt a new British station heavy cruiser.

segments.summary: The need for affordable station flagships could drive British heavy-cruiser development independently of treaty limits.

segments.title: Britain's construction reflex and Japan's sense of security
segments.body: Naval construction was an ingrained British political response to economic and strategic crises, illustrated by the prewar campaign that turned competing proposals for four or six ships into an order for eight. Japan's problem was different: money alone could not compress the 8-8 program into the promised schedule because its supporting industrial capacity was limited. Completing the program later on Japanese terms might leave leaders feeling less dictated to and somewhat more secure. Japanese extremism would remain, while treaty politics and industrial pace could still alter later diplomatic behavior.

evidence.note: Britain's habitual response to crises through naval construction and the political campaign that increased an order from four or six ships to eight.
Japan's industrial capacity constrained the pace of its 8-8 plan, while completion on its own schedule might have improved Japanese perceptions of security.

segments.summary: The counterfactual combines Britain's habitual use of naval construction with a slower Japanese 8-8 program pursued without the humiliation of imposed ratios.

segments.title: A purpose-built carrier race without treaty conversions
segments.body: The Royal Navy might move from Hermes and its conversions toward larger carriers with stronger decks, armor, bigger lifts, and larger air groups, improving designs through repeated construction. The United States would have a harder political case without foreign carrier programs to point to, but naval aviators and Pacific war games still provide evidence for a large carrier. Once either navy builds a battlecruiser-sized carrier, the other has an incentive to answer it. The competition therefore shifts carrier development from treaty opportunism toward a continuing contest over survivability, air-group size, speed, and range.

evidence.note: British designs could develop larger air groups, stronger decks, armor, and bigger lifts through repeated carrier construction.
American funding, naval aviation advocacy, and war games could support a large carrier; either a British or American design would invite a qualitative response from the other navy.

segments.summary: British carrier experiments and American war games could drive competing purpose-built designs even without Lexington and Saratoga conversions.

segments.title: Fleet strength as deterrence and diplomatic leverage
segments.body: Sustained construction could replace much of Britain's First World War-era battle fleet by 1940 while leaving additional ships in reserve, allied service, or modernization cycles. Such strength would make sanctions, patrols, and intervention more credible because Britain would possess both working flotillas and the capital ships that signaled resolve. Maintaining reserves and activating them for exercises could demonstrate readiness at less cost than fighting a war. A fleet could influence negotiations without combat because everyone knew it could be activated. Germany is still expected to turn toward Nazism in this scenario, while Japan and Italy could face materially different choices when weighing expansion against stronger maritime powers. An outmatched Germany might instead concentrate on submarines, prompting Britain to build more sloops.

evidence.note: Fleet replacement and greater reserve strength could give larger British and American fleets enough weight to alter Japanese and Italian calculations.
Maintained reserves and visible fleet strength could support diplomacy, while a German turn toward submarines could prompt British sloop construction.

segments.summary: A larger, newer Royal Navy could change Japanese, Italian, and German calculations by making intervention and escalation visibly more costly.

segments.title: Why Spanish Civil War patrols needed status ships
segments.body: The Spanish Civil War provides a practical example of fleet strength as diplomacy. British and French patrols needed destroyers for daily work, yet treaty limits left too few larger ships available to give those patrols political weight. Italian and German noncompliance was harder to challenge when the enforcing navies could not display enough force. A capital ship could function as a status asset, making the patrol's backing visible without firing its guns.

evidence.note: Destroyers performed patrol duties, while a shortage of larger ships reduced the visible force behind British and French pressure on Italy and Germany.

segments.summary: Spanish Civil War patrols show how destroyers could perform the mission while larger ships supplied the visible diplomatic pressure.

segments.title: London Treaty failure and Depression spending
segments.body: A failed first London Naval Treaty is more politically plausible than a missing Washington Treaty because Italy and Japan could simply decline to join. Treaty limits also restricted Britain's habitual use of warship construction and deployment as diplomacy while the United States remained outside the League of Nations. During the Great Depression, governments could direct money into shipbuilding and yard upgrades instead of paying to close or shrink industrial capacity. The Town-class cruiser example shows how yard selection was already tied to economic distress. Roosevelt's naval background and opposition to cumulative limits make renewed American construction politically easier to imagine.

evidence.note: A scenario in which the Washington Treaty survives but the London Treaty fails resembles the later breakdown of treaty limits.
Great Depression policy could direct money into shipbuilding and infrastructure, as the economic logic behind Town-class yard allocation illustrates.
Hoover, Roosevelt, and cumulative treaty limits in relation to renewed naval construction.

segments.summary: A failed London Treaty scenario turns Great Depression shipbuilding into a practical policy lever for Britain and the United States.

segments.title: Japanese 18-inch ships as the trigger
segments.body: Japan moving first after a failed London framework would set the technical terms of the next building round. An announced 18-inch-gun Japanese design would make British 12-inch, 14-inch, and other small battleship ideas politically and strategically difficult. Britain might answer with a fast design carrying new 15-inch/50 guns supported by existing shell stocks and barrel repair facilities. The United States would likely continue around 16-inch guns in triple turrets.

evidence.note: Reluctance to order first, a possible earlier Japanese 18-inch program, and competition for industrial capacity between capital ships and other ship types.
An announced Japanese 18-inch program could rule out Britain's smaller battleship proposals and favor new 15-inch/50 guns supported by existing ammunition and barrel facilities.
Likely American 16-inch triple-turret choices contrasted with Number 13-style ships planned for 30 knots and eight 18-inch guns in four twin turrets.

segments.summary: Japan building an 18-inch-gun capital ship would force Britain and the United States away from smaller treaty-style battleship ideas.

segments.title: New 15-inch guns supported by a global ammunition system
segments.body: An early Japanese 18-inch ship could prompt Britain to prioritize a fast response using new 15-inch/50 guns. A revived F3-style design, possibly enlarged to carry twelve guns, is one proposal. Existing 15-inch shell stocks around the world and the barrel repair, recasting, and sustainment industry would support it. Britain would need to retain older battleships until replacements arrived, so the proposed gun could also offer those ships an upgrade path. This scenario begins before the historical 14-inch program had matured, and the proposed 15-inch/50 response was not adopted historically.

evidence.note: A proposed F3-derived design with new 15-inch/50 guns could use established shell stocks and barrel repair and recasting capacity.
Retained battleships would need upgrades while replacements were built, before the historical 14-inch program reached maturity.

segments.summary: Existing shells and barrel facilities could favor a new British 15-inch gun program for both new ships and upgrades to older battleships.

segments.title: Fast battleships expose dock and canal constraints
segments.body: A 30-knot Japanese capital ship would pressure both Anglo-American navies toward fast battleships, but their infrastructure constraints differ. American dimensions remain tied to the Panama Canal, while Britain must consider dry docks distributed across a global operating system and may have to fund new floating docks. France and Italy would also need answers even though their armament and industrial bases could not simply copy the largest Japanese design. Paper specifications therefore lead directly to the expensive shore infrastructure required to build, repair, and deploy a fleet.

evidence.note: The Panama Canal constrained American dimensions, while Britain's global dry-dock limits might require investment in floating docks.
France and Italy would also need answers even though their armament and industrial bases could not simply copy the largest Japanese design.

segments.summary: Responding to a fast Japanese capital ship would force the United States, Britain, France, and Italy to reconcile fleet designs with canals, docks, armament capacity, and national industry.

segments.title: Carrier aviation and industrial spillovers
segments.body: Ark Royal, the Yorktown class, Implacable, and Midway represent different directions for carrier development. Continued programs could strengthen the case for earlier Royal Navy control of the Fleet Air Arm and push single-engine aircraft toward higher power-to-weight ratios because carrier deck and hangar space are scarce. Engine and aircraft research would employ specialists and could spread into motor and civilian industries. Secure contract workers are also more likely to spend wages locally, keeping money in circulation during an economic downturn. Bank deposits can return to circulation through lending, whereas cash kept at home does not. Many working-class households in the 1920s and 1930s lacked ordinary bank accounts, so uncertain income could lead to cash being kept at home instead of circulating through purchases.

evidence.note: Expanded naval aviation could stimulate engine research and spill into civilian industry, even though British and American carrier requirements differed.
Confidence in continued employment encourages spending, with a distinction between bank lending and cash hoarding, while service recruitment creates housing and infrastructure demand.

segments.summary: More carrier construction could advance naval aircraft, engine power, fleet-air organization, and civilian industry while circulating wages through the Depression economy.

segments.title: Strike carriers, armored fleet carriers, and air-group size
segments.body: British carrier requirements distinguished strikes against ships sheltering in harbor from operations close to the fleet and shore-based aircraft. The fleet-carrier role called for armor, particularly in the Mediterranean and South China Sea. Strike and fleet carriers could operate together in groups to compensate for the smaller air groups associated with survivability measures. Ark Royal exemplifies the strike role in this comparison, while designs resembling Implacable offered another direction for development. Midway is interpreted as extending the Yorktown approach with greater protection, while Essex gives more weight to rapid mass production. Britain and the United States could pursue these carrier programs alongside capital-ship construction more readily than Japan.

evidence.note: British strike and fleet-carrier roles, armor against shore-based threats, and combined groups compensating for smaller individual air groups.
Implacable-like designs and the comparison of Yorktown, Midway, and Essex, alongside Britain's and America's greater construction capacity.

segments.summary: Carrier roles shaped the balance between aircraft capacity and protection, with different British and American routes toward larger, more survivable ships.

segments.title: How non-treaty navies widen the building race
segments.body: The counterfactual extends beyond Britain, the United States, Japan, France, and Italy. German construction, Australian and New Zealand fears about Japan, Canadian preferences, and South American prestige purchases all create additional demand for ships and equipment. Canada might avoid a capital fleet yet still build destroyers and sloops suited to Atlantic service. The economic ripple therefore includes export yards and smaller navies responding to a world in which the major fleets are visibly expanding.

evidence.note: Germany, the Dominions, and Canadian destroyer and sloop forces would become further participants in the changed naval market.
South American governments might commission new warships despite weak finances when other navies resumed construction.

segments.summary: German, Dominion, and South American procurement could spread demand beyond the five powers usually associated with the naval treaty system.

segments.title: Arms-race knock-on effects before World War II
segments.body: Expansion by one navy drives construction elsewhere. A Japanese battleship program could push Soviet naval planning earlier, leave Germany further behind, and make Britain and France harder targets in the 1930s. Continuous programs might also expand testing and experimentation, although an early correction of the United States Navy's torpedo problems remains doubtful. Naval aircraft-engine research beginning around 1931 could leave Germany with more ground to recover when open rearmament began. More expenditure would still leave institutional problems unresolved, including the French Army's difficulties with radios. War could still follow, with different naval and industrial positions reshaping crises such as Abyssinia and the course of German rearmament.

evidence.note: Japanese construction might prompt earlier Soviet battleship decisions and further construction by other powers.
Germany's later naval rearmament could leave it further behind, while better American torpedo testing remains an explicitly doubtful possibility.
Greater British strength at Alexandria, competing Italian naval expenditure, and gradual infrastructure investment could alter the Abyssinia crisis and later rearmament costs.
Stronger Polish forces, Japanese fleet tradeoffs, and higher Italian and German rearmament costs could change the timing and alignment of war.
Earlier naval engine research could widen the lead over Germany, while higher spending would leave some institutional weaknesses, including French Army radio problems.

segments.summary: Earlier naval construction could alter Soviet, German, Italian, and British choices before World War II.

segments.title: Why four Japanese yards did not mean four ships at once
segments.body: Japan had four yards physically capable of building very large capital ships, but their supporting industry limited how many could progress together. The estimate is roughly three ships under active construction at any one time. Increasing that rate required investment beyond the yards themselves. New steel plants and other supporting facilities took time to build, so additional funding could not immediately remove the bottleneck.

evidence.note: Four nominally capable yards translated into an estimated three active capital-ship builds because expanding supporting industry required time.

segments.summary: Supporting industry could limit simultaneous capital-ship construction even when four Japanese yards had enough physical space.

segments.title: A stronger fleet at the Abyssinia crisis
segments.body: The Abyssinia crisis supplies a concrete test for the claim that fleet size changes diplomacy. Britain historically considered intervention but doubted that it could concentrate overwhelming force at Alexandria; years of uninterrupted construction could alter that calculation or deter Mussolini earlier. Italian naval spending might also compete with the resources required for the invasion itself. Gradual British infrastructure investment from the early 1930s could reduce the costly emergency acceleration that began historically in 1937. Roosevelt might use the same naval competition to justify American infrastructure spending.

evidence.note: Greater British strength at Alexandria and competing Italian naval expenditure could alter the outcome of the Abyssinia crisis.
Gradual infrastructure investment could reduce the need for Britain's urgent historical rearmament after 1937.

segments.summary: Gradual naval expansion could give Britain more credible force at Alexandria during the Abyssinia crisis while reducing the cost of the later emergency rearmament surge.

segments.title: Rearmament exports could strengthen Poland
segments.body: Naval rearmament affects land strategy through industrial scale and export capacity. If Britain and France are already producing ships, aircraft, and related equipment, third countries can buy from mature lines at lower cost. Poland has reason to procure earlier because Soviet pressure exists before Nazi Germany becomes the immediate western threat. A better-equipped Polish state is one factor that could make German invasion harder or delay the wider conflict.

evidence.note: Larger Allied production could make exports cheaper, enable earlier Polish procurement, and make a German invasion more difficult.

segments.summary: Larger British and French production runs could lower export costs and let threatened states such as Poland buy more ships, aircraft, and other equipment before 1939.

segments.title: The opportunity cost of Japanese super-battleships
segments.body: The no-treaty scenario does not automatically make every part of the Imperial Japanese Navy stronger. Concentrating scarce industrial capacity on large capital ships could reduce the carriers, cruisers, and destroyers available for operations beginning in 1937. Trying to preserve the carrier force as well would deepen the pressure on the rest of the fleet. The result might be superior individual fast battleships but a less balanced force facing an American demand for numerical superiority in its own fast-battleship program.

evidence.note: Japanese capital-ship construction could displace carriers, cruisers, and destroyers, while American planners would seek numerical superiority in fast battleships.

segments.summary: An earlier Japanese capital-ship program could produce impressive headline ships while weakening the carrier, cruiser, and destroyer balance needed for an effective fleet.

segments.title: The Pact of Steel and the cost of catching stronger rivals
segments.body: A British success during the Abyssinia crisis could push Mussolini toward another confrontation or persuade him that Italy could not afford one. British naval expansion and stronger French capital ships would make joining the Pact of Steel a more costly decision. Germany would also need to spend more to reach the strength required to fight France and Britain. Earlier Polish purchases from expanding Allied production lines could raise the cost of German aggression further. Germany's need to finance rearmament would still exert pressure toward war, leaving the outcome uncertain.

evidence.note: Alternative Italian reactions to an Abyssinia setback, the Pact of Steel, and the challenge posed by larger British and French fleets.
German rearmament's financial pressures and the added difficulty of confronting a Poland equipped through earlier foreign purchases.

segments.summary: Stronger British, French, and Polish forces could raise the price of aggression while making Italy's alliance choice harder to predict.

segments.title: Why the counterfactual cannot yield precise job totals
segments.body: Precise employment or spending totals are unavailable because the counterfactual fleet programs cannot themselves be known. A failed London Treaty stays closer to the historical design base and permits more bounded guesses, while a missing Washington Treaty changes American appropriations and British, Japanese, and French responses too early for confident ship lists. A Republican Congress might refuse further construction after the Lexingtons and South Dakotas, only to reconsider when foreign designs appeared. Gun caliber, speed, logistics, dock capacity, and the results of weapons testing all feed back into later choices. Japan's preference for funding warships over expanding the industry beneath its yards adds another constraint. These mechanisms reveal plausible pressures, but they cannot produce exact forecasts.

evidence.note: Exact economic totals and later fleet designs are uncertain, including American appropriations after completing existing programs.
Later outcomes would depend on interacting design choices, weapons trials, global logistics, dockyard capacity, and Japanese industrial limits.

segments.summary: Precise economic totals remain out of reach because changing treaty outcomes also changes politics, designs, infrastructure, and procurement sequences.

segments.title: Gun-barrel wear and Britain's global supply lines
segments.body: Lower expected barrel wear favored Britain's use of 45-calibre rather than 50-calibre guns. Longer barrel life mattered when ships operated far from the infrastructure needed to supply replacements. Fewer replacements meant fewer heavy barrels moving backwards and forwards around the world. The choice therefore affected the workload of support facilities and the fleet's supply system.

evidence.note: The preference for 45-calibre barrels is connected to reduced wear, longer service life, and fewer worldwide barrel shipments.

segments.summary: Longer barrel life could reduce replacement shipments for a navy operating far from its gun-support facilities.

segments.title: From naval wages to local spending and tax receipts
segments.body: Predictable naval orders give yards and suppliers confidence in employment across armaments, machinery, boilers, plumbing, furniture, aviation, and electronics. Workers then spend on food, housing, entertainment, transport, and consumer goods, supporting jobs beyond the naval supply chain. Most major powers would place much of the work in their own economies, although imports could carry some spending abroad, as with possible Italian purchases of British turbines. Foreign naval demand could add export work for the supplying country. Contracts also create legal and civil-service work, while employment turns benefit recipients into taxpayers. This spending could ease an economic downturn, though warship construction alone would not cure the Great Depression.

evidence.note: Stable shipyard and supplier work would carry naval spending into household purchases, while major powers placed most construction within their own economies.

Import leakage and export demand shape the spending multiplier; confidence in continued income encourages purchases, while naval contracts also create legal and civil-service work and turn benefit recipients into taxpayers.

segments.summary: Dependable naval contracts carry public spending into households, civilian employment, exports, and tax receipts.

segments.title: Could stronger fleets deter or fragment a world war?
segments.body: The naval treaty system restricted tonnage in pursuit of peace, yet it ultimately failed to preserve peace. Larger fleets might make aggression prohibitively costly and deter it. They might instead divide conflict into separate regional wars that could be contained before they combined. A third outcome is the historical global conflict in a different form. The counterfactual leaves the result open.

evidence.note: Treaty failure to preserve peace, higher conflict costs as a possible deterrent, and separate regional wars as an alternative to another global war.

segments.summary: Larger fleets might deter dictators, keep regional wars from merging, or reproduce World War II in a different form.
